report.answer_text:
On April 2, 2025, President Trump announced a two-part tariff package that he called "Liberation Day."
1. A universal baseline tariff
A 10% tariff applied to all imports beginning April 5.[1]
Executive Order 14257 raised tariffs on nearly all countries to 10% starting April 5.[2]
2. Higher country-specific "reciprocal" tariffs
Some countries faced additional reciprocal tariffs of varying rates, effective April 9.[1]
The reciprocal rates ranged from a flat 10% up to 50%.[3]
Countries facing rates above 10% included the European Union, China and Israel.[4]
The method appeared to take each country's trade deficit with the US, halve it, and apply that as the tariff.[5]
The country-specific rates were inclusive of the 10% baseline.[5] The two were not stacked.
The reciprocal tariffs did not replace earlier country-specific tariffs.[1] Many countries therefore faced combined rates well above 10%.
Related measures and exceptions
The 25% tariffs on foreign cars and auto parts, announced earlier, took effect at midnight.[4]
Canada and Mexico had separate treatment. USMCA-compliant goods stayed at 0%, and non-USMCA-compliant goods faced 25%.[6]
What happened afterward
Within a week, the administration announced a 90-day pause on the country-specific reciprocal rates. That dropped most countries to the 10% baseline, while China's elevated rates stayed in place.[7]
Trump later ordered the country-specific reciprocal tariffs to resume on August 7, 2025.[2]
I haven't covered later developments, such as court challenges to the tariffs or negotiated deals. I can look into those if you want.
